subject: Computer Networking
title: From 1G to 4G
description: A quick win: understand From 1G to 4G.

hook.text: In 1983, the first cell phone weighed two pounds and could only make voice calls. That was 1G.

buildup.text: 2G introduced digital voice and text messages in 1991. GSM became the global standard.

discovery.text: 3G arrived in 2001 with data speeds fast enough for basic web browsing and email on a phone.

twist.text: 4G LTE launched around 2010 and delivered broadband-level speeds — streaming, gaming, and video calls went mobile.

climax.text: Each generation took about a decade. Every step brought a 10x speed increase and entirely new use cases.

punchline.text: Each 'G' didn't just add speed. It unlocked new possibilities.

quiz.question: What did 2G introduce that 1G couldn't do?

details.summary: Cellular technology evolved from analog 1G voice in the 1980s to digital 2G that added text messaging, 3G that introduced mobile internet, and 4G LTE that brought broadband-speed data to phones. Each generation was defined by a leap in capability: voice, then data, then internet, then broadband.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding cellular generations explains the progression from voice-only phones to always-connected smartphones. Each generation enabled new applications that transformed mobile computing.
takeaways: 1G was analog voice only, with no encryption or data
2G introduced digital voice, SMS, and basic data services
4G LTE delivered broadband speeds that enabled the smartphone era

faq.question: What made 4G LTE different from 3G?
faq.answer: 4G LTE used an all-IP architecture that treated voice as just another data service. OFDMA modulation and MIMO antennas delivered speeds ten times faster than 3G. Latency dropped below 50 ms. This performance enabled video streaming, video calling, and app stores to flourish on mobile devices.

faq.question: Why were older cellular standards shut down?
faq.answer: Carriers reclaim spectrum from older standards to deploy more efficient technologies. 3G spectrum can serve far more 4G or 5G users. Maintaining legacy networks is expensive. Most devices have been upgraded. 2G networks persist in some regions for IoT devices and basic emergency connectivity.
